{{short description|Gauges opinion before and after significant deliberation}}
{{Broader|Citizens' assembly}}

A '''deliberative opinion poll''', sometimes called a '''deliberative poll''', is a form of [[opinion poll]] taken before and after significant [[deliberation]]. Political scientist [[James S. Fishkin]] of [[Stanford University]] first described the concept in 1988. The typical deliberative opinion poll takes a [[Simple random sample|random]], representative sample of citizens and engages them in deliberation on current issues or proposed policy changes through small-group discussions and conversations with competing experts to create more informed and reflective public opinion.<ref name="Luskin">{{cite journal |last=Fishkin |first=J.S. |author2=Luskin, R.C. |author3=Jowell, R. |year=2000 |title=Deliberative polling and public consultation |journal=[[Parliamentary Affairs]] |volume=53 |issue=4 |pages=657–666 |doi=10.1093/pa/53.4.657}}</ref> Deliberative polls have been run around the world, including recent experiments to conduct discussions virtually in the United States, Hong Kong, Chile, Canada and Japan.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Online Deliberation Platform |url=https://deliberation.stanford.edu/tools-and-resources/online-deliberation-platform |access-date=2023-09-15 |website=Deliberative Democracy Lab - Stanford University |language=en}}</ref>

==Process==
The Deliberative Democracy Lab at Stanford University described its process as:<ref>{{Cite web |date= |title=CDD: Deliberative Polling®: Executive Summary |url=http://cdd.stanford.edu/polls/docs/summary/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150210030843/http://cdd.stanford.edu/polls/docs/summary/ |archive-date=2015-02-10 |access-date= |website=Center for Deliberative Democracy}}</ref>

# A random, representative sample is first polled on the issue(s)
# Members of the sample are invited to gather in order to discuss the issue(s) (online or in-person)
# Carefully balanced briefing materials are sent to the participants and are also made publicly available (along with other aspects of the deliberations).
# The participants talk to competing experts and political leaders, asking questions they develop in small group discussions with trained moderators.
# The sample is again polled (with a private questionnaire) on the original questions. The resulting changes in opinion represent the conclusions the public would likely reach, if they had opportunity to participate in the deliberative process. By measuring both before and after judgments, policymakers and the media have more insight into the process and its impacts on participants.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Fishkin |first=James S. |title=Democracy when the people are thinking: revitalizing our politics through public deliberation |date=2018 |publisher=Oxford university press |isbn=978-0-19-882029-1 |location=Oxford |chapter=Ch. 1}}</ref>

Fishkin argues that during deliberation, discussions should strive for [[political equality]], where everyone's voice is given equal consideration. This can be achieved through discussions that:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Fishkin |first1=James S. |last2=Luskin |first2=Robert C. |date=2005 |title=Experimenting with a Democratic Ideal: Deliberative Polling and Public Opinion |url=https://www.uvm.edu/~dguber/POLS234/articles/fishkin.pdf |journal=Acta Politica |volume=40 |issue=3 |page=285 |doi=10.1057/palgrave.ap.5500121 |s2cid=144393786 |access-date=February 19, 2018}}</ref>
* are backed by reasonably truthful claims,
* give space for arguments both for and against the proposal,
* remain polite and listen to others,
* focus on the merit of the arguments, and
* cover a diverse array of perspectives from substantial portions of the population.

Logistically, deliberative opinion polls are very similar to other deliberative gatherings like [[Citizens' assembly|citizens' assemblie]]s.<ref name=":1">Scheufele, Dietram A. [https://nrs.harvard.edu/URN-3:HUL.INSTREPOS:37376270 "Modern Citizenship or Policy Dead End? Evaluating the need for public participation in science policy making, and why public meetings may not be the answer."] Shorenstein Center Research Paper Series 2011.R-34, January 2011. (note: not peer-reviewed)</ref> A couple areas where deliberative polling might differ is that a deliberative poll always has 100 to 200 participants, to ensure a statistically significant sample. In addition, deliberative polling emphasizes measuring opinion change after receiving new information and discussion rather than finding common areas of agreement or concrete policy proposals.<ref name="Luskin" /> The goal is to allow the researcher to get a reliable estimate of citizens' preferences both as-is and after an extensive process of deliberation about an issue.<ref name="Asahi">{{cite web |last=Tsuruoka |first=Masahiro |title=INTERVIEW: James Fishkin: Deliberative Polling should be used in key policy issues like energy |url=http://ajw.asahi.com/article/views/AJ201202240067 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304061106/http://ajw.asahi.com/article/views/AJ201202240067 |archive-date=4 March 2016 |access-date=12 November 2012 |publisher=[[The Asahi Shimbun]]}}</ref> Experiments in online polling using an AI moderator have led study authors to conclude that the AI model tested was as effective as human moderators according to participant evaluations, allowing polls to be conducted more often at a reduced cost.<ref name=":0">{{Citation |last1=Gelauff |first1=Lodewijk |chapter=Achieving parity with human moderators |date=2023-06-08 |title=The Routledge Handbook of Collective Intelligence for Democracy and Governance |pages=202–221 |edition=1 |place=London |publisher=Routledge |language=en |doi=10.4324/9781003215929-15 |isbn=978-1-003-21592-9 |last2=Nikolenko |first2=Liubov |last3=Sakshuwong |first3=Sukolsak |last4=Fishkin |first4=James |last5=Goel |first5=Ashish |last6=Munagala |first6=Kamesh |last7=Siu |first7=Alice|doi-access=free }}</ref> While in-person deliberations should pay for childcare, venues, moderators, hotels, and stipends to achieve a representative sample, [[online deliberation]]s seem to only need to offer increased bandwidth, technical support, newer devices and a smaller stipend to participants.<ref name=":0" />

== Examples ==

=== Online ===
In 2019, the Deliberative Democracy Lab and the Helena Group launched [[America in One Room]], a deliberative poll of a representative sample of 526 Americans on various issues.<ref>{{Cite news |last1=Badger |first1=Emily |last2=Quealy |first2=Kevin |date=2 October 2019 |title=These 526 Voters Represent All of America. And They Spent a Weekend Together |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/10/02/upshot/these-526-voters-represent-america.html}}</ref> Polling results found that in general voters seemed to move towards the center after their experience, with an effect lasting at least one year after the in-person gathering.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fishkin |first1=James |last2=Siu |first2=Alice |last3=Diamond |first3=Larry |last4=Bradburn |first4=Norman |date=November 2021 |title=Is Deliberation an Antidote to Extreme Partisan Polarization? Reflections on "America in One Room" |journal=American Political Science Review |language=en |volume=115 |issue=4 |pages=1464–1481 |doi=10.1017/S0003055421000642 |issn=0003-0554|doi-access=free }}</ref> Subsequent deliberative polls have been conducted online in groups of 10 using an AI moderator.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Fishkin |first1=James |date=August 21, 2023 |first2=Larry |last2=Diamond  |title=Can deliberation cure our divisions about democracy? |url=https://www.bostonglobe.com/2023/08/21/opinion/2024-elections-partisanship-democracy-common-ground/ |access-date=2023-09-11 |website=The Boston Globe |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== In person ===
In the mid-to-late 2000s, Fishkin's team selected a representative sample of the Chinese coastal township of Zeguo (pop. 120,000) in [[Wenling]]. Deliberative polling took place over a one- to three-day period after which recommendations were implemented. Most accounts found the pilot successful, leading to an expanded scope beyond public works projects to a process that determined the budget each year.<ref name="ISSUES">{{cite journal |last=Klein |first=Joe |author-link=Joe Klein |date=September 13, 2010 |title=Tough Issues |url=http://www.time.com/time/politics/article/0,8599,2015481,00.html |url-status=dead |journal=[[Time Magazine]] |page=29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100904075123/http://www.time.com/time/politics/article/0,8599,2015481,00.html |archive-date=September 4, 2010}}</ref><ref>Leonard, Mark. [https://www.prospectmagazine.co.uk/essays/52281/chinas-new-intelligentsia "China's new Intelligentsia"], [[Prospect (magazine)|''Prospect Magazine'']], Issue 144, 2008</ref>

Between 1996 and 1998, Fishkin managed deliberative opinion polls for electric utilities in Texas as part of the state's [[integrated resource planning]] process. The participants underwent a significant shift in the percentage who agreed that it was worth higher costs to invest in [[Efficient energy use|energy efficiency]] and renewable resources. Those findings led to a higher renewable energy portfolio standard, shifting the utilities' focus toward energy efficiency and renewables, resulting in a [[Wind power in Texas|relatively high percentage of wind power]] compared to other states.<ref name=ISSUES /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=McGrath |first=Mike |date=2020 |title=Deliberative Polling and the Rise of Wind Power in Texas |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.32543/naticivirevi.109.1.0034 |journal=National Civic Review |volume=109 |issue=1 |pages=34–38 |jstor=10.32543/naticivirevi.109.1.0034 |issn=0027-9013}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Galbraith |first1=Kate |last2=Price |first2=Asher |date=2013-09-17 |title=Book Excerpt: How the Public Got Behind Texas Wind Power |url=https://www.texastribune.org/2013/09/17/book-excerpt-how-public-got-behind-tx-wind-power/ |access-date=2023-07-06 |website=[[The Texas Tribune]] |language=en}}</ref>

==Impacts==
===On decision-makers===
Deliberative polling can serve as important input mechanisms upstream in the policy making process.<ref name=":1" /> Fishkin does not advocate using deliberative polls for every public concern. For instance, crisis measures that demand instant decisions may not be appropriate.<ref name="Luskin" /> However, he advocates using it for most tasks,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fishkin |first=James |date=2018-12-20 |title=Response to Critics: Toward the Reform of Actually Existing Democracies |url=https://scholarlypublishingcollective.org/good-society/article/27/1-2/190/200919/Response-to-Critics-Toward-the-Reform-of-Actually |journal=The Good Society |language=en |volume=27 |issue=1–2 |page=193 |doi=10.5325/goodsociety.27.1-2.0190 |issn=1089-0017|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which could include the hiring of crisis managers.

Some, like Lafont, see voting where everyone can participate as more legitimate than random selection of decision-makers. Fishkin believes that once most skeptics experience a well-run deliberative process that they would find it more legitimate than elections. Both believe that legitimacy is improved if the public can see all the inputs (including briefing materials) that led to the decision, so that others can be included in the reasoning for and against to know whether their views were given a fair hearing.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fishkin |first=James |date=2018-12-20 |title=Response to Critics: Toward the Reform of Actually Existing Democracies |url=https://scholarlypublishingcollective.org/good-society/article/27/1-2/190/200919/Response-to-Critics-Toward-the-Reform-of-Actually |journal=The Good Society |language=en |volume=27 |issue=1–2 |pages=196–200 |doi=10.5325/goodsociety.27.1-2.0190 |issn=1089-0017|url-access=subscription }}</ref> As both group dynamics and personalities of participants can play an important role in producing different outcomes of discussions, implementation is important for successful, legitimate deliberation.<ref name="Merkle" /><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last1=Binder |first1=Andrew R. |last2=Scheufele |first2=Dietram A. |last3=Brossard |first3=Dominique |date=April 10, 2012 |title=Opinion: Misguided Science Policy? |url=https://www.the-scientist.com/news-opinion/opinion-misguided-science-policy-41134 |access-date=2023-07-07 |website=[[The Scientist Magazine]] |language=en |type=Op-ed}}</ref><ref name="Admir">{{cite journal |last=Admir |first=J. G. |year=1996 |title=The Hawthorne effet is a common artifact in social research |journal=Public Perspective |volume=7 |pages=14–16}}</ref>

===On participants===
Participants can come to learn and appreciate the circumstances and interests of competing arguments through extended discussions and deliberations. This can be achieved by:
# randomly assigning participants into small groups and 
# having impartial moderators to ensure all the major arguments for and against major policy options are covered.<ref name="Luskin" />

While participants become more engaged and knowledgeable, thoughtful conclusions are expected to emerge, leading to a better quality of public opinion.<ref name="Merkle">{{cite journal |last=Merkle |first=D. M. |year=1996 |title=The polls - Review - The National Issues Convention Deliberative Poll |journal=Public Opinion Quarterly |volume=60 |issue=4 |pages=588–619 |doi=10.1086/297775}}</ref> Fishkin has found that if people think their voice actually matters in the question at hand, then they'll study the material, ask tough questions and think for themselves with about 70% changing their minds in the process.<ref name="ISSUES" /> Furthermore, it is also hoped that such poll can help increase deliberation among all members of the public.<ref name="Luskin2">{{cite journal |last=Luskin |first=R. C. |author2=Fishkin, J. S. |year=1998 |title=Deliberative polling, public opinion, and democracy: The case of the National Issues Convention |journal=Working Paper, University of Texas at Austin}}</ref> This led Fishkin and [[Yale Law School|Yale Law]] Professor [[Bruce Ackerman]] to propose a national holiday called [[Deliberation Day]] to allow voters to gather in large and small groups to discuss political issues.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Ackerman |first1=Bruce |author-link1=Bruce Ackerman |last2=Fishkin |first2=James |date=January 1, 2004 |title=For a Smarter Public, Deliberation Day |url=http://prospect.org/cs/articles?articleId=6960 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110810225708/http://prospect.org/cs/articles?articleId=6960 |archive-date=2011-08-10 |access-date=2023-07-06 |website=[[The American Prospect]]}}</ref>
